opus-5.5.text:
I think luck is mostly a function of surface area. You can't control whether any one thing works out, but you can control how many shots you take and how visible you are when you take them.

For me, a lot of it came down to doing things in public. When I was teaching myself ML outside the big labs, I'd write up what I was working on, put code out there, and just try to do genuinely interesting work where other people could see it. Most of that goes nowhere. But every so often someone you really respect stumbles across it, and that one interaction changes your whole trajectory. From the outside it looks like luck, but you've stacked the deck by having a hundred little things floating around for them to find.

The other half is being agentic about which problems you pick. A lot of people wait to be told what's important. If you develop your own taste, ask "what's actually the bottleneck here?" and go after it hard, you end up in the right place at the right time more often than chance would suggest. You notice a gap before it's obvious, so when the field catches up, you're already there.

And then there's just persistence. You have to be willing to work really hard on something for a long time without much external validation. The people who seem lucky are often the ones who kept going for a year after most people would have stopped, so they were still standing there when the opportunity showed up.

So I'd say: maximize your surface area, develop taste so you aim at the right things, and outlast people. Luck does the rest, but you've given it a lot more chances to find you.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes doing genuinely interesting work in public so respected people may discover it, presenting visible, attention-worthy work as a way to create more opportunities for luck.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is that luck is mostly a function of how many shots you take and how visible those shots are. When I look back at the moments that actually changed my trajectory, almost none of them were planned. They came from putting something out into the world and having the right person happen to see it.

So the practical version is: do a lot of things, and do them in public. Write up the half-finished experiment. Post the weird result. Send the cold email to the person whose paper you liked. Each of those individually has a low probability of going anywhere, but you only need one or two to hit, and the hits compound. Someone notices you, that leads to a conversation, that conversation leads to a collaboration, and suddenly you're working on something you never would have picked on your own.

The other piece is being in a position where you can actually catch the luck when it arrives. That means having enough slack in your schedule and enough breadth in your skills that when an interesting opportunity shows up, you can say yes and be useful immediately. A lot of people miss opportunities not because they didn't get them, but because they were too locked into something else to take them.

And then there's a selection effect on environment. If you're in a place where lots of ambitious people are working on hard problems, the base rate of lucky collisions is just much higher. Part of manufacturing luck is choosing to be somewhere dense with the kind of people and problems you want to collide with, even if the specific role you take there isn't the perfect one.

The last thing I'd say is that you have to be a bit shameless about it. Most people are too worried about looking naive or getting ignored. But the downside of a cold email that gets no reply is basically zero, and the upside is occasionally enormous. Once you internalize that asymmetry, it becomes very hard to justify not taking the shot.

r001.rationale: The response recommends putting research work into public view—such as writing up experiments or posting results—so the right person may notice it and create opportunities.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is increasing the number of opportunities you have to be surprised. You have some hypothesis about how a model works, you run an experiment, and something weird happens. It’s tempting to treat that as an obstacle to getting the result you wanted. But sometimes the weird thing is much more interesting than your original question.

So you want a fast loop where you can try lots of things, but you also need enough slack to stop and ask, “Why did that happen?” If you’re just running experiments without really looking at the results, you’re buying lottery tickets and never checking them.

The other part is being around people who notice different things than you do. You mention some strange result, and someone says, “Oh, that might connect to this other problem.” That can turn an observation you would have discarded into a direction worth pursuing.

You can’t guarantee an important discovery. But you can make yourself more likely to encounter something interesting, and better prepared to recognize it when you do.

r001.rationale: The response describes increasing chances of noticing unexpected results and benefiting from others’ perspectives, but does not present producing attention-worthy work as a way to manufacture research luck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is increasing the surface area for something interesting to happen. You try things, you talk to people, you follow up on results that seem a little surprising. Each individual attempt might have a low probability of going anywhere, but you get more chances to notice something useful.

The other part is being prepared to act on it. If an experiment behaves strangely, do you understand the system well enough to figure out whether that’s a bug or something worth investigating? And do you have enough room in your schedule to spend a few days finding out?

So I’d try to build a loop where you can test ideas cheaply, get feedback quickly, and change direction when the evidence is interesting. You can’t guarantee a discovery, but you can put yourself in a position where a lucky observation has somewhere to go.

r001.rationale: The response describes increasing opportunities to notice and investigate surprising results, but it does not present producing attention-worthy work as a way to manufacture luck.
